stories.title_en: Splitting USB-C: USB 3 and USB 2 on one port

comments.author: jsmith45
comments.text:
While this does largely work, there are a few complications.
The biggest one being power management, especially the cutting off of power to a specific port. If a host wants to cut off power to a 3.x device, it typically needs to know which 2.x port that device is connected to. The host internally can have some really wild mappings of 2.0 and 3.x hubs, controllers, etc, but the device tree or ACPI tables let it know exactly which ones are paired together for any port leaving the device. After that point it is assumed that the host can learn the topology from any hubs attached. The power management is tied to the 2.0 port. Unexpectedly splitting the topology could lead the host to instruct a hub to cut off power to the wrong port when trying to target a specific USB 3.x device.
Also, if a hub indicates that a device is drawing excessive current, and there is nothing communicating on the 2.0 lines, there is a risk of the wrong 3.x getting blamed by the host, possibly showing a warning popup to the user with the wrong device name, or similar.
This isn't to say this is always a problem, because it isn't but it is something to be aware of.

comments.author: derf_
comments.text:
It is surprisingly easy to get unexpected negative values with floating point operations. One I remember was a square root that was failing on a negative argument
despite that argument being clamped against zero
. The problem was that the clamp was using some macros
#define MIN(a, b) ((a) < (b) ? (a) : (b))
#define MAX(a, b) ((a) < (b) ? (b) : (a))
and the arguments were being clamped with MAX(x, 0). Well, if x is
negative zero
, it is not less than 0, so the macro returns x. The square root then looks at the sign bit and fails. Negative zero is a perfectly possible result from a series of calculations that destructively cancel.

comments.text:
The problem with this AI generated animation is that the watch wont work - unless the balance wheel happens to be a perpetuum mobile.
Now if you ask the AI a specific question about the energy flow in this system, the AI will immediately answer what it got wrong: the balance wheel needs to have the energy replenished every half cycle.
And for that to happen, the pallet fork must have a) jewels and b) a specific shape to give a tiny push to the wheel once a tooth is unlocked. [1]

He starts with the most basic movements, and works you up to what would still be considered modern technology discounting Spring Drive and some other hot rod timepieces.

comments.author: jstanley
comments.text:
Nice work, but it looks to me as if the escape wheel is unable to provide any impulse to the pallet so I think this watch will not work with the pallets shaped as shown.
After unlocking, the tooth of the escape wheel needs to press against the pallet, which will press against the impulse jewel, to add some energy to the balance, otherwise the balance will come to a stop.
It would be good to be able to slow down the animations to check this.
The escapement really has two jobs. One is to limit the rate at which the mainspring can unwind, and the other is to supply energy to the balance so that the balance keeps swinging.

comments.author: rippeltippel
comments.text: I am currently job hunting and the identity crisis is real. Some interviewers want candidates to go agents all the way down, summoning code fire-and-forget. Other ones require checking all the generated code before each commit. I sit in the middle of that spectrum and, since there's no consolidated right or wrong practice and no one knows in advance what any interviewer would prefer, interviews are now mostly a matter of luck. The problems mentioned in the article seem to me a consequence of that crisis: how much agency should agents have? The spectrum of possibilities is wide and mostly discretional.
